CHIEF COMPLAINT
Worsening headaches over the past few months and newly diagnosed pituitary lesion.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
52-year-old male referred by Dr. Henry Howard for neuro consultation regarding newly discovered pituitary lesion and possible surgical intervention. Patient presented to primary care on 3/1/21 complaining of worsening headaches over several months. Headaches began approximately 3 months ago with gradual onset, initially rated 3/10 severity and progressively worsened to 6/10 severity. Pain is described as dull, nagging ache located behind the eyes, worse in the morning, lasting a few hours at a time. Nothing makes pain better or worse. Patient denies associated nausea, fever, rash, neck stiffness, numbness, weakness, or syncope. Recently noticed bumping into door frames. Denies fever, rash, or neck issues. Workup for headaches included brain MRI with contrast and serology studies. MRI performed 3/4/21 reveals pituitary lesion with elevation and compression of the optic chiasm. Ventricles normal in size with no other abnormalities noted. Patient attempted Tylenol for headaches without relief and discontinued use.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Denies fever, rash, neck stiffness, numbness, tingling, or syncope. Denies nausea or feeling sick. No recent vision changes noted; eyes were last checked in fall. Recently experiencing difficulty with peripheral vision, bumping into door frames. Denies balance problems.

PAST MEDICAL HISTORY
Unremarkable. No known medical problems.

MEDICATIONS
No current medications. Tried Tylenol for headaches without benefit.

ALLERGIES
Not discussed.

FAMILY HISTORY
Patient was adopted and has no knowledge of family medical history.

SOCIAL HISTORY
Works as a computer programmer. Married for 25 years. Recently purchased a small house. Denies alcohol use, tobacco use, and recreational drug use, never has used any of these.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Patient alert and oriented to time, place, and person. Affect appropriate, speech fluent. Cranial nerves grossly intact. No focal motor or sensory deficit in upper or lower extremities. Visual acuity and eye movements normal. Pupils equal and reactive. Visual field testing reveals bitemporal hemianopia. Color vision normal.

RESULTS
CBC, comprehensive metabolic panel, coagulation studies, and CRP all normal as of 3/3/21. Pituitary hormone profile demonstrates low TSH; all other results normal. MRI brain with contrast from 3/4/21 shows well-defined pituitary mass with compression of the optic chiasm. Ventricles normal in size. No other abnormalities noted.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
Benign-appearing pituitary adenoma incidentally discovered during workup for worsening headaches. Patient is symptomatic with clinical and radiographical evidence of optic chiasmal compression. Surgical intervention indicated. Plan for transsphenoidal approach to excise adenoma and decompress pituitary fossa. Patient counseled on surgical risks including anesthesia-related risks (heart attack, stroke, death), infection, need for further surgery, wound complications (CSF leak, infection requiring prolonged hospitalization), seizure, stroke, permanent neurological deficits (numbness, weakness, difficulty speaking), and death. Patient to see surgery scheduler (Deborah) to schedule procedure expeditiously. Patient will also be scheduled for visual field testing today or tomorrow to establish baseline peripheral vision prior to surgery for comparison postoperatively. Referral to ophthalmology for full eye exam and formal visual field testing. Specimen will be sent to pathology for definitive diagnosis. Patient counseled that vision improvement is possible but not guaranteed.
